item.title: Earth has a New Moon
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
"Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN:
Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun.
The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October.
While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar...
The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system.

item.title: Bitcoin Drops to $56,085, a Two-Year Low, in Worst Month Since 2022
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Seven days ago Slashdot reported Bitcoin had plummeted 24% in just 46 days. Since then it's dropped another 9.4%, falling to $56,085 by Friday night, its lowest price in over two years. "It has lost more than half its value since reaching a peak above $126,000 in October 2025," reports Bloomberg, noting it's now worth less than when Donald Trump first took office in January of 2025.
Yahoo Finance reports:
At its current price, the digital coin is down more than 20% so far in November, putting it on pace for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, according to Yahoo Finance data. That would be bitcoin's eighth-worst month since Yahoo Finance's daily records began tracking the digital asset in September 2014...
US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds have also added to the selling pressure. So far this month, net investors have withdrawn roughly $3.5 billion, according to asset manager Farside Investors, which tracks the product flows. That includes $582 million in outflows on Thursday alone.

item.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.
The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED.
"We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."

item.title: AI Made Us Faster. So Why Do Designers Have Less Time?
item.author: Rinat Seif
item.content:encoded: A poster that used to take me a day now takes a minute to generate. Last night I built an animated website in one evening without writing a single line of code. By every estimate, designers should have half their lives back.Yet I haven't met a single designer who has more free time. Deadlines are shorter, revisions are longer, and by the evening there are so many options that your eyes start to blur.So I tried to figure out what is going on. Are we bad at working with AI? Were we sold a fantasy? Or is this just a bubble that is about to pop? The answer turned out to be more interesting than all three.It feels faster. It turns out slowerIn 2025, researchers at METR ran a simple experiment. Sixteen experienced developers worked on real tasks, some with AI tools and some without. Before they started, they expected AI to make them 24% faster.With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The strangest part: even after the experiment, they believed AI had made them 20% faster.The study is small, and it is about developers, not designers. But the same picture shows up in much larger surveys:2,500 workers and executives in 4 countries96% of executives expect AI to raise productivity. 77% of employees say it added to their workload52 interviews, 300+ public AI initiatives95% of organizations got zero return from generative AIComputers went through the same thing in the 1980s. Economist Robert Solow famously observed that you could see the computer age everywhere except in the productivity statistics. The growth did come, but only after people rebuilt the way they worked.Where the saved time goesI see three reasons, and none of them is that the models are bad.1. Generation got cheap. Choosing didn't. A designer used to make three options and bring the best one. Now you can get 200 in an hour. Each one has to be looked at, compared, and rejected for a reason. Nobody counts that time, but it eats all the savings.2. Clients know generation takes a minute too. So "by Friday" turned into "by tomorrow", and one round of revisions turned into five. Economists call this the Jevons paradox: when something gets cheaper, we consume more of it. Cheap images didn't reduce the work. They increased the appetite.3. We dropped AI into the old process. Brief, references, sketches, approvals all stayed the same. There is just a new "generate" button in the middle. According to Upwork, 47% of employees using AI don't know how to reach the productivity gains their managers expect. And in the MIT report, the 5% of companies that succeeded rebuilt the process itself instead of buying one more tool.There is one more thing METR showed. With AI, the feeling of speed and actual speed drift apart. Generating gives you the sense that work is happening even when it is stuck. For designers, it looks like an hour of rerolling one frame instead of five minutes thinking about what exactly is wrong with it.Fair question. In June 2026, JPMorgan estimated global AI infrastructure spending at $5.5 trillion through 2030. The largest cloud providers alone are spending about $650 billion in 2026, increasingly with borrowed money. Investors argue about one thing: whether demand will catch up with the spending.For designers, I think something else matters more. Even if the financial bubble pops, the tools won't disappear. After the dot-com crash in 2000, the internet didn't go away. The companies that couldn't make money on it did, and the ones that could grew in their place.AI looks similar. If there is a bubble, it is in expectations: "buy a subscription and everything gets faster." The data above shows it doesn't work that way. But the change in the profession has already happened, and it won't roll back.More designers, less foundationThere is another tension in the industry. Open Threads and it looks like everyone is a designer now. The profession has ballooned and is changing in front of us. But behind a lot of those generations is a lack of basics: composition, grids, typography. AI doesn't fix that. It mass-produces it.That is especially true for product designers moving from interfaces into visual work. A component library keeps a UI consistent, but there is no Storybook for light, texture and framing.What I do to make the speed realI decide before the first generation, and I set a limit. Light, background, palette and grid are written down in advance. Only the object changes in the prompt. If three rerolls don't get the frame right, I stop and put into words what exactly is wrong. Every frame of the series on one screen, then I remove the one that doesn't fit. Comparing them one by one in a chat window takes many times longer. Three directions with a rationale, not a folder of 50 images. The more options a client sees, the longer they take to decide and the more revisions they send.None of these steps requires a new model. They are all about who is running the process.We weren't fooled. We were sold faster execution and assumed we had bought faster work. AI speeds up making things. It doesn't free up a designer's time on its own. The person who frees up time is the one who decided in advance what they are making and knows how to choose quickly.That animated website from the first paragraph took one evening for exactly that reason: I knew what feeling I wanted before I typed the first prompt. Without that, I would still be rerolling it.Has AI saved you time, or eaten it? And how have your deadlines changed in the last year?

"Should this run on Amplify, Lambda or ECS?" is usually answered with a feature list. I wanted numbers. So I took one Next.js app, deployed it to four AWS runtimes in the same account and Region, including the new Lambda Web Functions, and measured the things that decide the choice in practice: latency under load, cold starts, CPU speed, real limits, and the monthly bill at four traffic levels.Lambda and ECS run the exact same container image, and the Web Function runs the same files from a .zip. Amplify Hosting builds the same Git commit. Every command, script, and result is in a public repository, with deploy and cleanup steps: Four results surprised me:One ECS Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU was the fastest option for light requests, then failed completely under load: at 200 requests per second, 29% of page requests returned errors, and ECS replaced the overloaded task twice during my tests.Lambda, Lambda Web Functions and Amplify kept the same latency from 10 to 200 requests per second with zero errors.The new Web Functions had the fastest CPU and no 6 MB response limit, but in my test they cost about four times as much as classic Lambda, because idle environments are billed for memory.Amplify cuts every request at about 28 seconds and every response at 6 MB, and classic Lambda behind a Function URL also stops at 6 MB.One app, four runtimes, one DynamoDB table: builds the app from GitHub and runs the server-side code on its own managed compute. (a classic function, which AWS now calls an Event Function) runs the container image through the Lambda Web Adapter, exposed with a Function URL. Each execution environment handles one request at a time. run the same Next.js server from a .zip as a real HTTP server, with no adapter. Each environment handles many requests at once, and you pay for active CPU time instead of wall-clock time. runs the same image as a service behind an Application Load Balancer.The app has a few endpoints, each testing something different:: a server-rendered page that reads one DynamoDB item, the typical "real page": no I/O at all, to measure the runtime's own overhead: one DynamoDB GetItem, a typical API call: 50,000 chained SHA-256 hashes, to compare the CPU you actually get and : to find the real request timeout and response size limitEvery response reports which runtime served it, the CPU architecture, and whether it was the first request of that process (a cold start):{"runtime":"lambda","cold":true,"requestsServed":1,"arch":"arm64","node":"v22.23.5","memoryMb":1024} 2. Prerequisites and costAn AWS account and the AWS CLI v2 with credentials for it. Web Functions need a recent version with the commands (I used 2.40.4); run to check.Docker with buildx, Node.js 22, and k6 for the load testsA GitHub account for Amplify HostingEverything runs in eu-central-1. Lambda and Fargate use arm64 (Graviton) and roughly the same size: Lambda with 1024 MB of memory, and a Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB. A Web Function environment has a fixed size of 2 arm64 vCPUs and 2 GB, which you can't change, and Amplify chooses its own compute.While the setup is running, the only fixed cost is the ECS part: the load balancer, one Fargate task and four public IPv4 addresses, about $1.90 per day. Lambda, Amplify and DynamoDB cost close to nothing at test traffic. Run the cleanup script when you are done.3. The app and one image for two runtimesThe app is a normal Next.js app router project. The only special setting is the standalone output, which produces a small self-contained for the container. Amplify builds the app its own way, so the setting is applied only in the Docker build:const config: NextConfig = { output: process.env.STANDALONE ? "standalone" : undefined, poweredByHeader: false, }; The Dockerfile is where Lambda and ECS meet:FROM node:22-alpine COPY --from=public.ecr.aws/awsguru/aws-lambda-adapter:0.9.1 /lambda-adapter /opt/extensions/lambda-adapter WORKDIR /app ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 \ AWS_LWA_READINESS_CHECK_PATH=/api/health COPY --from=build /app/.next/standalone ./ COPY --from=build /app/.next/static ./.next/static RUN rm -rf .next/cache && ln -s /tmp/next-cache .next/cache USER node CMD ["node", "server.js"] The is copied into . Lambda starts everything in that folder as an extension, and the adapter turns each invoke event into a normal HTTP request to . On ECS, nothing starts it, so the same image is a plain web server.The points to a separate route. My first version used , and the adapter's readiness probe became the "first request" of every process, so no request ever looked cold. Health checks should not touch the code you measure.The is moved to , because Lambda's file system is read-only everywhere else.Build for arm64 and push to ECR:aws ecr create-repository --repository-name runtime-benchmark \ --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 --provenance=false \ -t "$REPO_URI:$IMAGE_TAG" --push . keeps a plain single-platform image. By default, buildx adds an attestation manifest and pushes an image index, which Lambda may refuse to use. The script tags each image with the Git commit, so an immutable tag always matches one commit.Scan on push found one critical CVE on the first push, in from the base image, not in the app. Base images are rebuilt on a schedule, so security fixes can be days old before they reach the tag you pull. One line in the final stage fixed it:RUN apk upgrade --no-cache The next image scanned with zero findings. The compressed image is 88 MB in ECR (233 MB unpacked).The DynamoDB table is on-demand with one item. Each runtime gets its own IAM role with exactly one permission, on this table.4. Lambda with a Function URLaws lambda create-function --function-name runtime-benchmark --package-type Image \ --code ImageUri="$REPO_URI:$IMAGE_TAG" --architectures arm64 \ --role "$ROLE_ARN" --memory-size 1024 --timeout 30 \ --environment "Variables={RUNTIME_NAME=lambda,TABLE_NAME=runtime-benchmark,APP_REGION=eu-central-1}"
aws lambda create-function-url-config --function-name runtime-benchmark --auth-type NONE aws lambda add-permission --function-name runtime-benchmark --statement-id public-url \ --action lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl --principal '*' --function-url-auth-type NONE aws lambda add-permission --function-name runtime-benchmark --statement-id public-invoke \ --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal '*' --invoked-via-function-url A public Function URL now needs both permissions: , and limited to calls that come through the URL. I removed the second one to check, and the URL answered with 403 and a helpful message:{"Message":"Forbidden. Invoking a Function URL requires both the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions."} A Function URL is free and needs no API Gateway. For production, you would usually put CloudFront in front of it for a custom domain, caching and AWS WAF.The quota that new accounts don't tell you aboutBefore load testing, check this:aws lambda get-account-settings --query 'AccountLimit.ConcurrentExecutions' 10 The documented default is 1,000 concurrent executions, but my account had 10. Ten concurrent requests at about 100 ms each is roughly 100 requests per second, and anything above returns . I requested an increase in Service Quotas (quota code L-B99A9384).The increase to 1,000 was approved automatically after 2 hours and 20 minutes. Lambda's fast endpoints need far less concurrency than you might expect: at about 40 ms per request, 50 requests per second keep only 2 to 3 environments busy. The CPU endpoint at 50 requests per second peaked at 57 concurrent executions, well over the original limit.Lambda Web Functions are a new kind of Lambda function for HTTP traffic. Your code is a normal web server that listens on a port, Lambda gives it an HTTPS endpoint, and each execution environment serves many requests at the same time, like a container. It still scales to zero when there is no traffic.Node.js only (), deployed as a .zip from a versioned S3 bucket. No container images.Arm64 only. Each environment has 2 vCPUs and 2 GB of memory, and you can't change that.Your server must listen on the address in () within 10 seconds of startup.Each environment handles up to 64 concurrent requests by default (maxConcurrencyPerEnvironment, 1 to 128), and Lambda lowers that limit dynamically based on resource usage.The Next.js standalone server reads and instead, so the entry file maps one to the other:// index.js: the Web Function entry file const [host, port] = (process.env.AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT || "localhost:3000").split(":"); process.env.HOSTNAME = host; process.env.PORT = port; require("./server.js"); To keep the comparison fair, I didn't rebuild the app. The deploy script copies out of the same linux/arm64 container image, adds , and deploys that folder:cid=$(docker create --platform linux/arm64 "$REPO_URI:$IMAGE_TAG") docker cp "$cid:/app/." build/web-function/ && docker rm "$cid" cp web-function/index.js build/web-function/
aws lambda-web deploy --name runtime-benchmark-web --code build/web-function \ --create --include-hidden-files \ --execution-role-arn "$ROLE_ARN" \ --env RUNTIME_NAME=lambda-web --env TABLE_NAME=runtime-benchmark --env APP_REGION=eu-central-1 \ --timeout-seconds 30 --endpoint-name main --auth-type ApplicationManaged is easy to miss: the Next.js build lives in , and without the flag the command leaves hidden folders out of the package. creates the S3 bucket, the function, the first revision and a public endpoint, and waits until the endpoint is active. My first deploy took under a minute.A revision is an immutable snapshot of code and configuration. Changing an environment variable means a new revision, and an endpoint can route traffic to one revision or split it between two, which gives you canary deployments without CodeDeploy.The pricing model is different from classic Lambda. In eu-central-1 you pay $0.30 per million requests, $0.000035 per vCPU-second of CPU time that your code actually uses, and $0.0000046 per GB-second of memory for the whole life of each environment. A request that waits for DynamoDB uses almost no CPU, so it costs very little. But an environment that stays alive costs memory time even between requests: one environment kept alive for a month is about $24 in memory alone.6. ECS Fargate behind a load balancer, without a NAT gatewayA Fargate task in a private subnet needs a NAT gateway or VPC endpoints to pull its image, and either costs more than the task itself. For this test, the tasks run in public subnets with a public IP, and the security groups do the protecting:The ALB security group allows port 80 from the internetthe task security group allows port 3000 only from the ALB security groupaws ecs register-task-definition --family runtime-benchmark \ --requires-compatibilities FARGATE --network-mode awsvpc --cpu 512 --memory 1024 \ --runtime-platform cpuArchitecture=ARM64,operatingSystemFamily=LINUX \ --execution-role-arn "$EXEC_ROLE_ARN" --task-role-arn "$TASK_ROLE_ARN" \ --container-definitions file://container.json
aws ecs create-service --cluster runtime-benchmark --service-name runtime-benchmark \ --task-definition runtime-benchmark --desired-count 1 --launch-type FARGATE \ --network-configuration "awsvpcConfiguration={subnets=[$SUBNETS],securityGroups=[$TASK_SG],assignPublicIp=ENABLED}" \ --load-balancers targetGroupArn="$TG_ARN",containerName=app,containerPort=3000 Two roles, two jobs: the execution role lets ECS pull the image and write logs, and the task role is what your code runs as. The DynamoDB permission goes on the task role only.Two settings save time on every deploy. The target group health check uses every 10 seconds with a healthy threshold of 2, so a new task gets traffic in about 20 seconds. The deregistration delay is 10 seconds instead of the default 300, so an old task stops quickly.One bug from my script is worth sharing: separates a list of subnet IDs with tabs, not spaces. My script turned spaces into commas, so the service request got one "subnet ID" with tabs inside and failed with Subnet ID must match subnet-[0-9a-f]+. Pipe the list through .Amplify Hosting connects to GitHub with its own GitHub App. It does not use an AWS CodeConnections connection, even if you already have one for CodeBuild or CodePipeline. So the first step is in the console: Create new app, GitHub, choose the repository and the main branch. Amplify detects Next.js and uses the from the repository.Environment variables don't reach your server codeThis is the biggest surprise for anyone coming from Lambda or ECS. Amplify passes environment variables to the build, not to the server-side code at runtime. The fix is to write the variables your server code needs into during the build:build: commands: - env | grep -E '^(RUNTIME_NAME|TABLE_NAME|APP_REGION)=' >> .env.production || true - npm run build The is there because my first build failed without it. Before the variables were set, found nothing and exited with code 1, and Amplify stopped the build with "Command failed with exit code 1".Two more rules: variable names can't start with , so the app reads instead of , and secrets should not go into this way, because they end up in the build artifact.The server-side code needs AWS credentials to call DynamoDB. Amplify calls this a compute role: an IAM role that can assume.aws iam create-role --role-name runtime-benchmark-amplify-compute \ --assume-role-policy-document file://amplify-trust.json aws amplify update-app --app-id "$APP_ID" --platform WEB_COMPUTE \ --compute-role-arn "$COMPUTE_ROLE_ARN" \ --environment-variables RUNTIME_NAME=amplify,TABLE_NAME=runtime-benchmark,APP_REGION=eu-central-1 Without a compute role, the page renders but the DynamoDB call fails with a credentials error.The first response from Amplify answered a question the console doesn't:{"runtime":"amplify","cold":true,"arch":"x64","memoryMb":1024} AWS_LAMBDA_FUNCTION_MEMORY_SIZE is set, so the server code runs on Lambda with 1024 MB, on x64, managed by Amplify. You can't choose the memory size or arm64, and it doesn't count against your account's Lambda concurrency quota. k6 on a laptop in London, against the default URL of each runtime. Absolute latencies include my network path; the differences between runtimes are what matter. a constant arrival rate (k6 ) of 10, 50 and 200 requests per second for 2 minutes per endpoint, with p50, p95 and p99. for Lambda, the script changes an environment variable before each request, which retires all warm environments, and repeats this 10 times. For Amplify, it sends one request after 20 minutes of no traffic. ECS has no cold starts while a task runs. and with increasing values.k6 run -e BASE_URL=$URL -e ENDPOINT=/api/item -e RATE=50 -e DURATION=2m bench/load.js bench/coldstart.sh lambda 10 bench/limits.sh lambda $URL At 10 requests per second (p50 / p95 / p99 in milliseconds, 1,200 requests each):On light requests, ECS is the fastest, Lambda and the Web Function are close behind with almost the same medians, and Amplify is about 1.5 times slower than Lambda. ECS wins here because nothing sits between the load balancer and a warm Node.js process.The CPU row is the surprise. One Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU could not keep up with 10 CPU-heavy requests per second: each request needs about 80 to 150 ms of CPU, so the work arrived faster than half a vCPU could do it. Requests queued, the ALB health checks timed out, and ECS replaced the "unhealthy" task in the middle of the test. 8% of requests failed and the median rose to 1.9 seconds. Lambda, the Web Function and Amplify handled the same load without errors, because they add execution environments as the load grows.The lesson is not that ECS is slow. A fixed-size service needs auto scaling and headroom, and a health check that shares the CPU with the work it checks can turn an overload into a restart.At 200 requests per second (p50 / p95 / p99 in milliseconds, 24,000 requests each):Lambda, the Web Function and Amplify barely noticed the twentyfold increase: their medians moved by a few milliseconds and no request failed. For the Web Function, I ran the 200 requests per second test twice, because AWS says the first load test on a new Web Function scales conservatively, and the table shows the second run. The two runs were within a few milliseconds of each other. Lambda scaled to 234 concurrent executions in the first seconds of the test, then settled between 50 and 90, with zero throttles.The single ECS task reached 100% CPU and failed. At 50 requests per second the same task used about 65% CPU on the page endpoint, so one 0.5 vCPU task handles roughly 70 page requests per second before it falls over. For real traffic, you would run at least two tasks with target tracking auto scaling at 50 to 60% CPU.The 50 requests per second results look like the 10 requests per second ones for Lambda, ECS and Amplify, so I left them in the repository instead of adding another table.One more number explains why Lambda looks so fast: its billed duration (the CloudWatch Duration metric) was 9 to 16 ms at the median for the light endpoints. Most of the 40 ms that the client sees is the network and the Function URL, not your code.The CPU endpoint does the same 50,000 hashes everywhere: about 150 ms billed duration per request, 155 to 182 ms at the clientWeb Function, 2 vCPUs, arm64: 96 to 102 ms at the median at the client, the fastest of the four 204 to 217 ms at the clientFargate, 0.5 vCPU, arm64: 79 ms for a single request on an idle task, but it cannot sustain that: at 10 requests per second the task collapsedLambda gives CPU in proportion to memory: one full vCPU at 1,769 MB. At 1024 MB you get a bit more than half a vCPU, and you pay for the milliseconds you use. A Web Function environment always has 2 vCPUs, and you pay only for the CPU time you use. Node.js runs JavaScript on one thread, so a single request can use only one of them, but that one is a full vCPU. Fargate gives you exactly the vCPU you reserve, all the time, whether you use it or not.Lambda, 10 forced cold starts (the script changes an environment variable before each request):Init Duration in the Lambda logs: 768 to 941 ms, about 820 ms at the medianFirst request at the client: 1.04 to 1.36 s, about 1.1 s at the medianThe next request on the same environment: 100 to 195 msThe very first cold start after deploying a new image took 3.7 s of init and 4.2 s at the client, because Lambda had not cached the new image yetAmplify, one request after 20 minutes without traffic, 3 times: 1.94 s, 2.00 s and 0.33 s, compared with about 0.16 s for a warm request. All three were served by a new process, so the third one probably landed on an environment that Amplify had already prepared. You can't see or control this, so plan for about 2 seconds on the first request after a quiet period.Web Function, 5 forced cold starts (each run creates a new revision, which starts new environments):First request at the client: 0.95 to 1.21 s, about 1.02 s at the medianThe next request on the same environment: 140 to 300 msAfter the 200 requests per second test ended, the environments stayed alive for about 5 minutes before Lambda removed them. One environment that I woke up with 7 requests stayed alive for more than 6 minutes. A site that gets a request every few minutes will rarely see a Web Function cold start, and that matters for the cost below.ECS has no cold start while a task is running, which is what you pay the fixed monthly price for. Scaling out is a different story: in the ECS events, a replacement task registered with the load balancer about 25 seconds after it started, and then needed two 10-second health checks before it got traffic. A new Lambda environment was ready in about one second.I asked each runtime to wait longer and longer, and to return larger and larger responses: Lambda stopped at 30 seconds with 502, which is the function timeout I configured; you can raise it to 15 minutes. The Web Function stopped at 30 seconds with 504 and the header lambda-web-error-type: Runtime.RequestTimeout; its also goes up to 15 minutes. ECS stopped at 60 seconds with 504, the ALB idle timeout, which you can raise to 4,000 seconds. Amplify stopped every request at about 28 seconds with 504, and you can't change that. Lambda returned 5 MB but failed at 6 MB with 502, the payload limit for buffered responses. Amplify also returned 5 MB and failed at 6 MB, with 413. ECS returned 20 MB without trouble, because nothing between the ALB and the container limits the size. The Web Function also returned 20 MB, because it streams responses by default.If your app has report downloads, file exports or slow third-party calls, these limits decide more than any latency number. Classic Lambda can go beyond 6 MB with response streaming, but that needs code changes. With Web Functions, you get it without changes.10. What it costs per monthPrices are on-demand prices in eu-central-1 from the AWS Price List API, in November 2026, without free tiers: $0.20 per million requests plus $0.0000133 per GB-second. The Function URL is free.Lambda Web Functions (arm64): $0.30 per million requests, $0.000035 per vCPU-second of CPU time actually used, and $0.0000046 per GB-second of memory for the whole life of each environment. Each environment has 2 GB, so one environment that stays alive all month costs $24.35 in memory. $0.30 per million requests plus $0.20 per GB-hour, which is about $0.0000556 per GB-second, 4.2 times the Lambda arm64 rate. Data out is $0.15 per GB, and builds are $0.01 per minute. Fargate arm64 at $0.03725 per vCPU-hour and $0.00409 per GB-hour, so one 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB task is $16.58 per month. The ALB is $0.027 per hour ($19.71 per month) plus LCUs. Public IPv4 addresses are $0.005 per hour each: the ALB has one per Availability Zone and each task has one, so four addresses add $14.60 per month.What my Web Function test actually costWeb Functions publish their own usage in CloudWatch (, and in the namespace), so I could calculate the real bill for my load tests instead of estimating it:147,608 requests in about 20 minutes3,966 vCPU-seconds of CPU, which is 27 ms per request on average48,354 environment-seconds (13.4 environment-hours) at 2 GB eachCost: $0.04 for requests, $0.14 for CPU, $0.45 for memory, $0.63 in total, or $4.28 per million requests71% of the bill was memory. At 200 requests per second, Lambda ran up to 55 environments, and none of them served more than 2 requests at the same time (the EnvironmentConcurrentRequests maximum). That was the case in both 200 requests per second runs. AWS documents that a new Web Function starts with a conservative per-environment concurrency limit and raises it as it learns, but I didn't see that happen in about 25 minutes of testing. About 30% of the memory time came after the test, while the environments waited about 5 minutes before Lambda removed them.The same request mix on classic Lambda would cost about $0.15, or $1.04 per million requests. So in my test, Web Functions cost about four times as much. If the per-environment concurrency grows over time, as AWS describes, this gap will shrink, so treat it as the cost of a new function under a load test, not a final verdict.Monthly cost at four traffic levelsFor the monthly bill, I used the measured durations: 20 ms of Lambda billed time per request (the 9 to 16 ms median, rounded up), and 5 KB per response. Amplify doesn't publish its billed compute time per request; its CloudWatch Latency metric averaged about 100 ms, which includes the CDN, so I show 100 ms as the upper bound and 30 ms as a likely lower bound. ECS uses the measured capacity of about 50 requests per second per task with headroom. For the Web Function, I used 27 ms of CPU per request, at least one environment alive all month (requests arrive more often than every 5 minutes at these levels), and the measured 0.24 environments per request per second at steady load.ECS has a floor of about $57 per month before the first request: $16.58 for the task, $19.71 for the ALB, about $6 for LCUs and $14.60 for four public IPv4 addresses. A second task for availability adds about $20.Web Functions have a soft floor of about $24 per month, one 2 GB environment kept alive by regular traffic. With traffic that stops for long periods, the environment scales to zero and the floor disappears. Above that floor, the CPU-based billing is cheap: 10 million requests add only about $12.Lambda stays cheapest until about 100 million requests per month for this light app. 100 million requests is 38 requests per second on average, so a real service would hit that level only with steady traffic.Heavy requests make both more expensive. At 150 ms per request (the CPU endpoint), Lambda costs about 7.5 times more than at 20 ms. But one 0.5 vCPU task sustains only about 3 such requests per second, so ECS needs many more tasks too. Per request they end up close, and Lambda still has no monthly floor.The script is in the repository (), so you can run it with your own durations and response sizes. for a frontend-first app with light server-side code, when you want Git push to production with preview branches and no infrastructure work. Check the 28 second and 6 MB limits against your app first, and remember that it runs on x64 and its compute costs about four times as much per GB-second as Lambda on arm64.Choose Lambda Web Functions for Node.js web apps that need more than classic Lambda allows: responses over 6 MB, streaming, CPU-heavy requests (2 vCPUs per environment gave the fastest CPU results), or canary deployments between revisions without extra tooling. It needs no adapter and scaled to 200 requests per second with zero errors. Watch the memory bill: in my test, idle environments made it about four times as expensive as classic Lambda, so check after your first week. for APIs and server-rendered pages with spiky or low traffic. It scaled from 10 to 200 requests per second with no errors and no configuration, and costs almost nothing when idle. Design for cold starts of about one second, the 6 MB response limit, and check your account's concurrency quota before launch. for steady traffic, long requests, large responses, WebSockets or background work, and when you need private networking to a database. It had the lowest latency per request. But plan the capacity: run at least two tasks, add auto scaling, and accept the monthly floor.The same build runs on classic Lambda, Web Functions and ECS, so this is not a one-way decision. The Web Function in this article is the same folder as the container image, plus a 5-line . Starting on Lambda and moving when your traffic or your limits change is a reasonable path.APP_ID=d123abc infra/cleanup.sh The script deletes the Amplify app, the ECS service, cluster, load balancer and target group, the Lambda function, the Web Function and its code versions in the shared bucket, the security groups, the ECR repository, the DynamoDB table, the log groups and the IAM roles. Everything it created has the tag project=runtime-benchmark, so you can check in Tag Editor that nothing is left.The feature lists told me that ECS is "more powerful", Lambda is "serverless" and Amplify is "easy". The measurements told a more useful story. The always-on container was the fastest per request and the first to fail, because one task is a fixed amount of CPU. The three serverless options were a little slower per request but did not care whether traffic was 10 or 200 requests per second. The newest one, Lambda Web Functions, removes most of classic Lambda's limits and was the fastest on CPU, but its memory billing made it the most expensive serverless option in my test. And the limits that matter most for real apps, request timeout and response size, differ by an order of magnitude between them.If you only take one thing from this article: measure your own app on the runtime you plan to use, before you choose. The repository makes that a few commands, and the cleanup script removes everything when you are done.

item.title: Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports: A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins.
The Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away and a well-characterized astrophysical source of X-ray light. By observing it, the team can work out the performance characteristics of MIXS in space and compare these with calibration measurements made with the same instrument in the laboratory in 2015. These observations provide MIXS's first view of an astronomical X-ray source. The main observation sequence consisted of 55 spacecraft slews, with 39 hours of observations during Sept. 11-12. Measuring how much the Crab Nebula's image is spread across MIXS's detector helps the scientists measure MIXS's angular resolution, or how sharply it will be able to distinguish features on Mercury's surface. They found this to be slightly better than when it was last measured in the lab in 2015. "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out," said Professor Emma Bunch, Principal Investigator (PI) for the MIXS instrument and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester.
"We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after eight years in space. We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine-tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."

item.title: Your Win Rate Is Wrong Because of the Denominator
item.author: Malek Damiri
item.content:encoded: Ask three people in the same company for the win rate and you can get three answers, all calculated correctly, from the same CRM. The numerator is never the argument. Everyone agrees on what a won deal is. The fight is about the denominator: which deals count as a chance you had to win.That choice can move the number by half. It can also make a quarter look like a disaster when nothing about the sales team changed. Here's a simulated example, the three common formulas, and the one I'd put in front of a leadership team.I simulated two years of opportunities, about 9,000 of them. The rules never change:30% are disqualified on the first call and closed lost within ten days.12% are qualified, then go quiet. Nobody closes them out. They sit open.The rest get worked. Each has a 32% chance of being won, with a median cycle of about 60 days.On March 31, 2026, someone runs a pipeline cleanup and closes every quiet deal older than 90 days as lost.The sales team is exactly as good in every quarter. Any movement in the win rate is bookkeeping.This is the one most dashboards show. Of the deals that closed this quarter, what share were won?-- 1. The usual one: of the deals that closed this quarter, what share were won? select date_trunc('quarter', closed) as qtr, count(*) filter (where status = 'won') as won, count(*) as closed_deals, round(count(*) filter (where status = 'won') / count(*), 3) as win_rate from deals where status in ('won', 'lost') and closed >= '2025-01-01' group by 1 order by 1; qtr won closed_deals win_rate 2025-01-01 191 1019 0.187 2025-04-01 198 970 0.204 2025-07-01 217 984 0.221 2025-10-01 199 1019 0.195 2026-01-01 196 1767 0.111 2026-04-01 203 990 0.205 Two problems. First, the number is low, around 20%, because a third of the denominator is deals that were never real. Disqualifying a bad lead on the first call is good sales behavior, and this formula punishes it.Second, look at the first quarter of 2026. The win rate halves. Wins are flat at 196. What changed is that the cleanup dumped hundreds of old, quiet deals into the denominator on a single day. If this number goes in a board deck, someone will spend the next month explaining a collapse that never happened.The obvious fix is to drop the deals that were never qualified.-- 2. Same, but only deals that were ever qualified select date_trunc('quarter', closed) as qtr, round(count(*) filter (where status = 'won') / count(*), 3) as qualified_win_rate from deals where status in ('won', 'lost') and qualified and closed >= '2025-01-01' group by 1 order by 1; qtr qualified_win_rate 2025-01-01 0.292 2025-04-01 0.312 2025-07-01 0.339 2025-10-01 0.298 2026-01-01 0.136 2026-04-01 0.307 Better. The number now reflects deals that someone actually worked. But the cleanup quarter is still broken, and there's a quieter problem: in every normal quarter, this formula leaves out the deals nobody closed. They aren't won and they aren't lost, so they don't count. A team that never marks anything lost gets a flattering win rate for free.That's the real issue with any "closed this quarter" win rate. It measures when someone updated a field, not how deals turned out.The fix is to stop asking what closed this quarter and ask what happened to the deals created in a quarter. Every deal belongs to exactly one cohort, from the day it's created. It's in the denominator whether anyone ever closes it or not.-- 3. Cohort: of the qualified deals created in a quarter, what share were won, and how many are still open? select date_trunc('quarter', created) as cohort, count(*) as deals, round(count(*) filter (where status = 'won') / count(*), 3) as won_share, round(count(*) filter (where status = 'lost') / count(*), 3) as lost_share, round(count(*) filter (where status = 'open') / count(*), 3) as still_open from deals where qualified and created >= '2025-01-01' group by 1 order by 1; cohort deals won_share lost_share still_open 2025-01-01 785 0.247 0.753 0.000 2025-04-01 778 0.274 0.726 0.000 2025-07-01 800 0.258 0.743 0.000 2025-10-01 757 0.256 0.736 0.008 2026-01-01 777 0.245 0.535 0.220 2026-04-01 779 0.086 0.189 0.725 The cleanup has disappeared. Each cohort wins about 25 to 27% of its qualified deals, which is the honest answer: about 83% of qualified deals get worked and 32% of those win. Formula 2 said 30% because it quietly ignored the deals that went nowhere.The cost is that recent cohorts aren't finished. The April 2026 cohort shows 8.6% won, but 72% of its deals are still open. That's not a bad quarter. It's an unfinished one. So always show the still-open column next to a cohort win rate, and don't compare a cohort with its predecessors until it's mostly closed. In this data, that's about two quarters.Use the cohort win rate as the headline, on qualified deals, for cohorts that are at least 90% closed. It doesn't move when someone cleans up the CRM, and it counts deals that went quiet as what they are: deals you didn't win.Show the still-open share for recent cohorts, so nobody reads an unfinished cohort as a bad one.Keep the period win rate as an operational number, not a performance one. It's useful for checking how many deals the team is closing out each week. It's misleading as a measure of how good the team is.Write the definition down. "Win rate = won deals divided by qualified deals created in the period, measured once the cohort is 90% closed." One sentence settles most of the arguments before they start, and it means sales, marketing, and finance all quote the same number. If your company does periodic pipeline cleanups, and most do, any metric built on close dates will spike that quarter. Mark the date on the dashboard or, better, stop building performance metrics on close dates.Most broken ratios in revenue reporting are broken in the denominator. Win rate, conversion rate, churn rate, attainment: each one hides a choice about who was eligible. Before you trust a ratio, ask what's in the bottom half, and whether something other than performance could change it.

item.title: Fledge Launches World Connection Day on November 21 to Fight Loneliness
item.author: Technology Wire
item.content:encoded: New York, United States, November 20th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--, a dating app built on psychological compatibility, is launching World Connection Day (WCD) on November 21, 2026, a worldwide initiative encouraging people in cities across the US, Canada and Europe to meet new people in local squares, parks and waterfronts. The initiative aims to encourage social connection and address loneliness through simple, face-to-face interactions. Participation is free and does not require registration.On Saturday, November 21, 2026, people will head to local squares, parks and waterfronts wearing a colored ribbon on their wrist. There are four ribbon colors, and each participant receives theirs after a short, playful hello-style test.The color reflects how the person approaches a conversation and how ready they are to start one. Whatever the color, the ribbon means one thing - you can say hello to me. World Connection Day (WCD) is a worldwide day for meeting new people, started by Fledge, a dating app based on psychological compatibility.The idea comes from the same place as the app: the better you understand yourself, the easier it is to recognize who is right for you. Fledge puts psychological compatibility at the core of its product, matching people by how they think, communicate and connect rather than by photos alone. WCD brings that approach offline and the test shows people their own style of saying hello and which style pairs best with it, so the first step toward a stranger feels less like a gamble.Loneliness is no longer a niche topic. on Social Connection reports that 1 in 6 people worldwide experience loneliness, with loneliness linked to more than 871,000 deaths annually. The WHO also identifies loneliness and social isolation as factors that increase the risk of serious health problems, including cardiovascular disease, depression and anxiety. But loneliness also shapes everyday life.When something wonderful happens and there’s no one to call, small moments like that add up to a bigger question of whether you have people you can count on. Being single doesn’t automatically mean being lonely, because friends, family and community can all provide closeness. What matters is having relationships in which you feel known and accepted."Having spent years developing the dating app to bring people together, I know the main obstacle isn't discovering a match—it's breaking the ice," said Val Klimov, the founder of Fledge, whose platforms have reached 20 million users. "The ribbon removes that hesitation. Wearing it signals that you welcome a conversation. During initial testing at Web Summit, 35% of attendees selected red for the bold hello, while 30% picked blue for the deep hello. Courage takes different forms. Certain individuals take the lead, whereas others prefer a thoughtful prompt. Ultimately, no one wants to take that step alone."Find your ribbon color. A two-minute test of 10 everyday situations, developed by the Fledge team, reveals your “hello style.” Each color shows how you start a conversation, and each has a natural pair, the hello that gets a conversation going most easily:Red, the bold hello. The first move is always yours. Pairs with yellow.Yellow, the warm hello. People come to you to talk. Pairs with red.Blue, the deep hello. One real question instead of small talk. Pairs with green.Green, the easy hello. People find you easy to talk to. Pairs with blue.Choose a spot. Two official WCD spots are on the map for November 21: South Bend, Indiana and Limassol, Cyprus. People elsewhere can take part independently, wherever they are.Go out on November 21. Come at any time of day, wear the ribbon and say hello to anyone else wearing one. Participants get email reminders the day before and on the morning of the event.Keep the conversation going. The WCD site offers free tools for the first minutes after “hello”: four decks of question cards, 30 ideas for a couple of hours together, and a first line for each color.Every ribbon means the same thing: you can say hello to me. No color is a warning, so red isn’t “stop” and yellow isn’t “busy.” A ribbon means it’s okay to say hello, and “no, thanks” is a complete answer. If someone takes their ribbon off, it means “not now.” WCD takes place in public places, in daylight, and is for adults 18+. Volunteers can be on-site beacons with spare ribbons, and brands and venues can join through the site.One of the flagship WCD cities will be South Bend, Indiana. On November 21, Notre Dame hosts SMU at Notre Dame Stadium, and ribbons will be available to fans in South Bend on game day.World Connection Day is a worldwide initiative that will take place three times a year, bringing people together through simple, spontaneous encounters. The November 21 edition coincides with World Hello Day, observed since 1973, and features two official spots in Limassol and South Bend. Looking ahead, the team aims to expand the initiative ahead of its next editions on February 13, 2027, the day before Valentine’s Day, and June 21, 2027, the summer solstice, so that people experiencing loneliness around the world can find a nearby city and find WCD spots nearby. is a dating app designed to help people understand compatibility before they start dating. Going beyond attraction, Fledge uses a research-based approach that considers personality, values, and relationship preferences to identify who may genuinely be a good fit before the first message. The result is fewer, more meaningful matches and a calmer way to date at your own pace, with less pressure, less performance, and more space to be yourself.Fledge is built by serial entrepreneurs with experience creating dating products used by more than 20 million people, including one of Europe's top-10 dating platforms. Its compatibility model draws on established behavioral science, and the company intends to pursue independent research partnerships. Founded in 2026, Fledge is operated by Fleamily, Inc., a Delaware corporation based in New York. item.title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Slashdot has been covering the Riemann Hypothesis for years.
2000: Prove The Riemann Hypothesis And Make.Money.Fast 2002: More on Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Claimed Proof of Riemann Hypothesis 2008: Prominent Mathematicians Rebuke Recent Riemann Hypothesis Proof
Add a new headline to the list...
2026: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math's great mysteries
joshuark shares a report from Scientific American: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has claimed to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model Claude, but the proof is not yet independently verified and remains under scrutiny. [An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion.] The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order.
[...] Alpoge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI's mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. [...] Alpoge's statement is elegiac -- recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling -- but also optimistic. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light," he wrote, "but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." [...]
The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn't have any immediate real-world applications -- it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems." "If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. "Something like a Rosetta Stone."
"If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," added mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind.
In a separate article from Scientific American, independent mathematicians say the AI-assisted proof is almost certainly valid. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland said the chance of anything being wrong was "approximately zero" after independently compiling and checking the code. However, researchers are still conducting final checks to ensure the proof accurately represents the original hypothesis and does not exploit any loopholes in Lean's verification system.
But did a human beat the AI? The Washington Post reports:
Just hours after AlpÃgeâ(TM)s claim circulated on social media, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society and a professor at Stanford University, said in a hurried statement that mathematician Alessandro Masullo had a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis without AI several months earlier. The draft, which runs some 940 pages, is in need of significant revisions, Masullo said in a statement, and was not ready for publication. Online observers quickly noted that it contained omissions and apparent errors. But in the introduction to the draft, he published a striking flag. âoeIf any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this,â he wrote. âoeWe are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.â

item.title: FCC Backs AT&T's Plan To Remove Copper Landlines In California
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. In May, the company urged the commission to declare that federal laws preempted California's regulations, thus clearing the way for AT&T to discontinue the service as it prioritizes high-speed fiber and expanded 5G cellular coverage.
Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. "While we preempt those requirements that necessitate that AT&T obtain a variety of CPUC [California Public Utilities Commission] approvals before it can discontinue POTS [plain old telephone service] in accordance with federal authorization, we do not preempt the COLR and other obligations more generally," the 74-page document says.
[...] Despite the FCC's order, it's not entirely clear if AT&T will pursue the copper landline phase-out in California. In May, the carrier sued to overturn the local regulations and block the CPUC from enforcing them against AT&T, which noted it spends $1 billion each year to maintain the copper network. That court case remains ongoing. [...] According to the regulator, AT&T has proposed discontinuing the legacy telephone service in the state on or after June 1, 2027.

item.title: Your CRM Stage Probabilities Were Made Up - Calibrate Them in an Afternoon
item.author: Malek Damiri
item.content:encoded: Open your CRM's opportunity stages and look at the probability next to each one. Discovery 10%. Qualified 20%. Solution 40%. Proposal 60%. Negotiation 80%. Verbal 90%.Where did those numbers come from? In most companies, nobody knows. They were set when the CRM was implemented, often by copying a template, and they've never been checked. Yet, they drive the weighted pipeline number that shows up in forecast calls and board decks.Checking them takes an afternoon and one SQL query, as long as you have one thing: a snapshot of the pipeline at a fixed point in time.For each of the last several quarters, you need the list of deals that were open on the first day of the quarter, with the stage each one was in that day. Most CRMs keep field history, and most warehouses that sync a CRM keep daily snapshots. If you have neither, start saving a snapshot today and come back in two quarters.The first-day snapshot matters. If you look at deals in their current stage, you'll only see the deals that are still open or the stage they died in, which tells you nothing about how likely a deal was to close when it was at that stage.Then join each snapshot deal to how it ended: won at any point, and won in the same quarter.I simulated eight quarters of first-day snapshots, about 3,400 deal-quarters, with the usual 10/20/40/60/80/90 probabilities in the CRM and different true win rates underneath.-- for every deal open on the first day of a quarter: what share were eventually won, and won that same quarter? select stage, any_value(crm_probability) as crm_says, count(*) as deals, round(avg(won_ever::int), 2) as won_eventually, round(avg(won_this_quarter::int), 2) as won_same_quarter, round(sum(amount * won_this_quarter::int) / sum(amount), 2) as won_same_quarter_by_value from snapshots group by stage order by stage; stage crm_says deals won_eventually won_same_quarter won_same_quarter_by_value 1-discovery 0.1 1129 0.07 0.02 0.01 2-qualified 0.2 882 0.16 0.05 0.05 3-solution 0.4 644 0.28 0.14 0.14 4-proposal 0.6 421 0.47 0.31 0.29 5-negotiation 0.8 236 0.57 0.47 0.47 6-verbal 0.9 94 0.84 0.80 0.76 Two separate problems show up.The CRM's probabilities are too high even for eventual wins. A deal in Negotiation is won 57% of the time, not 80%. A deal in Solution is won 28% of the time, not 40%. This is common. Stage probabilities are usually set by optimists, and they're rarely lowered.The forecast needs a different number entirely. A stage probability answers "will this deal ever close?" A quarterly forecast needs "will this deal close this quarter?" Those differ a lot for early stages. A Solution-stage deal on the first day of the quarter has a 28% chance of eventually closing, but only a 14% chance of closing before the quarter ends. Early-stage deals take time.The last column weights by deal value. If it differs a lot from the deal count version, big deals behave differently from small ones, and you should calibrate by size band too.The real test is whether the measured rates forecast better than the CRM's. I learned the rates from the first four quarters and tested them on the last four, which is the honest way to check. Testing on the same quarters you learned from will always look good.-- weighted pipeline with the CRM's probabilities vs the measured ones, against what actually closed with rates as ( select stage, sum(amount * won_this_quarter::int) / sum(amount) as measured from snapshots where quarter <= 4 -- learn from the first four quarters group by stage ) select s.quarter, round(sum(s.amount * s.crm_probability) / 1e6, 2) as crm_weighted_m, round(sum(s.amount * r.measured) / 1e6, 2) as measured_weighted_m, round(sum(s.amount * s.won_this_quarter::int) / 1e6, 2) as actually_closed_m from snapshots s join rates r using (stage) where s.quarter > 4 -- and test on the last four group by s.quarter order by s.quarter; quarter crm_weighted_m measured_weighted_m actually_closed_m 5 4.60 1.82 2.01 6 5.19 2.11 2.37 7 4.35 1.71 1.91 8 4.61 1.85 1.98 The CRM-weighted pipeline says about $4.6 million every quarter. About $2 million actually closes. The CRM number is more than twice the truth. The measured rates come in about 10% low, close enough to be useful, and the error is consistent enough that you could see it and adjust after a quarter or two.A weighted pipeline that's off by more than 2x isn't just inaccurate. It's actively harmful, because people make hiring and spending decisions based on it.Things that will trip you up. If reps often jump deals straight to Proposal, the deals in Proposal on the first day are a mix of real proposals and deals that never had discovery. That's fine for calibration. You're measuring what Proposal means in practice, not in the sales playbook.Re-opened and recycled deals. If lost deals get re-opened later, decide whether a re-open is the same deal or a new one, and be consistent. If the stage definitions changed a year ago, only use quarters after the change. Fewer quarters of the right data beat more quarters of the wrong data. With 94 deals in Verbal across eight quarters, the 84% is reasonably solid. If a stage has 20 deals, the measured rate could easily be off by 15 points. Pool more quarters, or merge thin stages.Update the CRM probabilities to the eventual win rates. They're used in lots of places, and the eventual rate is what the field implies.Use the same-quarter rates for the quarterly forecast. Keep them in a small table in the warehouse, not in the CRM, and recompute them every quarter from the latest eight quarters.Show both numbers in the forecast meeting. "Weighted pipeline at the CRM's probabilities is $4.6 million. At measured rates, it's $1.8 million." The first time the meeting sees that, the conversation changes.Recalibrate on a schedule. Win rates drift as products, markets, and teams change. Put a calendar reminder at the start of each quarter.None of this needs a forecasting tool. It needs a pipeline snapshot, one query, and the willingness to replace a number everybody's used to with one that's right.I'm Malek Damiri, head of revenue operations in Atlanta. I write about pipeline, forecasting, and the numbers behind them at malekdamiri.com.
