item.title: The Shortest Games in a Game Backlog Are the Ones People Finish Least
item.author: NXTO
item.content:encoded: I expected "play the short ones first" to work. Data from 129 real game backlogs says short games get finished at a third of the rate of mid-length ones.Every guide to clearing a game backlog says the same thing: start with the short games, get quick wins, build momentum. I built a game backlog tracker, so I could check whether people actually do that.I joined each game with its HowLongToBeat main-story time and looked at what share ends up in "Done". The data is 129 accounts and 25,276 games, taken on 2026-11-10. Only games with a known length are counted.Finish rate by game length.The shortest games are the largest group by far (more than half of games with a known length), and they are the ones least likely to be finished. Mid-length games, 5 to 30 hours, are finished about three times as often.Why I think this happens (hypotheses, not findings). Short games are cheap, free, or arrive in bundles, so they land in the backlog without anyone deciding to play them. A 3-hour game gets played in one evening, and nobody comes back to update the status. A game you paid little for has little to make you start it.I can't separate these from the data. What the data does show is that "short" is not enough of a reason to pick a game.Finish rate by genre (genres with at least 800 games)Games with a clear end (platformers, shooters, horror) get finished more often than open-ended ones (strategy, simulation). That fits: if a game never really ends, "Done" is a decision, not an event.What I'd change in a backlog tracker because of thisDon't present length as the main way to pick. Length plus genre plus what you finished before is a better signal, which is also why recommendations here use your own finished and rated games.Treat "Done" for open-ended games as optional. A second status for "played enough" would be more honest.Make marking a short game as Done a single click at the moment you stop playing it. Small, self-selected sample. Many people imported whole Steam libraries, so "not done" includes games they never meant to play. Genres overlap (one game counts in several rows). The finish rate is a measure of what people recorded, not what they played.If you track your game backlog somewhere, I'd be curious whether your short games get finished.

item.title: Voice Biometrics: The Night Identity Finally Learned to Speak
item.author: @Vishal
item.content:encoded: Turning the new system on is the easy part. Turning the old one off is the hard part.Somewhere in your organization, a slide says voice authentication is live. A pilot ran. A few thousand people enrolled. But listen closely: the old identity system is still doing most of the talking. The promise of voice biometrics is simple. Your voice becomes your key. No PIN to remember. No knowledge-based questions. You speak, the system listens, and you are verified.Inside an enterprise, it rarely works that cleanly. A voice model can be accurate and ready for production while the identity infrastructure around it still runs on old assumptions. Legacy authentication stacks carry years of rules, exceptions, integrations, and fallback paths, some documented, many not. Voice biometrics is less of an authentication upgrade and more of an identity migration, and migrations tend to expose everything an organization forgot it had built.The old system never dies quietly.Every company has a legacy system that was supposed to be temporary. It gets patched. Then integrated. Then extended. Eventually nobody wants to touch it. Authentication systems are the worst of the breed: security, customer experience, fraud, compliance, and operations all meet in one flow, so one small change can rattle several of them.Picture a contact center adding voice authentication. A customer speaks a passphrase. The system compares the sample against the enrolled voiceprint. The score clears the threshold. Authentication succeeds. Except the legacy platform still asks certain customers for a PIN, or the IVR routes the call through an old knowledge-based step. The new system works. The customer still experiences the old one. That gap is the central problem in identity modernization: replacing the technology does not automatically replace the behavior.The ghosts in the identity machine.Dig into a mature authentication stack, and you find things that never appear on the architecture diagram. A stored procedure that applies a fraud rule to one category of account. An IVR route that behaves differently because of an incident from years ago. A customer segment on a different path because of a business rule nobody remembers writing. These are the ghosts. The trouble is that nobody remembers which behaviors are essential and which are accidents of history.You cannot safely replace what you do not understand, so before migrating, the team has to map more than the happy path: verification failures, fraud signals, incomplete customer data, agent overrides, different policies for different customers. Architecture diagrams describe systems. Production behavior describes reality. The two are not always the same.The seam that makes migration possible.Once you understand the old system, the next question is how to replace it without putting every customer interaction at risk. A big-bang cutover sounds simple on a whiteboard. At midnight, switch the traffic. In practice, it means bridge calls and rollback plans, with the team watching dashboards like heart monitors.There is a quieter approach. Teach the old system to speak. Every enrollment becomes an event. Every verification attempt, every failure, every fraud suspicion, every override. A stream of events feeds the new identity platform while the legacy system keeps making the production decisions. For a while, both run side by side. The old platform speaks. The new one listens. The new system is not trusted with customer decisions yet. It shows it understands the same environment without risking a single customer.Running the two systems side by side creates an opportunity: comparison. When the two platforms disagree about an authentication attempt, investigate. Maybe a legacy exception was never captured. Maybe the biometric confidence threshold needs another look. Without visibility into missing events, processing lags, and unreconciled records, parallel operation creates false confidence: the new platform can look healthy while quietly missing parts of the old system's behavior.A voice match is not an identity decision.Voice biometrics brings a distinction that catches teams off guard. A successful voice match and a successful identity decision are two different things. The biometric engine answers one question: does this voice match the enrolled voiceprint? A production identity system has to answer a broader one: given this result and everything else known about the interaction, should this customer be authenticated?The verification flow therefore combines the biometric score with audio quality, fraud signals, and transaction context. The score is only one input. Teams that wire it straight to "authenticated" end up surprised the first time a noisy call, a bad cold, or an unusual transaction arrives. Voice biometrics is one signal in the identity decision, not a standalone feature.Voice adds a new dimension to fraud. An attacker does not need a perfect copy of a customer's identity. The system only has to be fooled. Recorded voices can be replayed. Synthetic voices improve every year. Attackers probe audio conditions and weak spots in the authentication flow, so the defenses have to cover replay detection, rate limiting, risk-based checks, and anomaly monitoring alongside voice similarity.Biometric confidence is not fraud risk. A system can be highly confident a voice resembles an enrolled voiceprint and still flag the interaction. A low score, on the other hand, does not mean fraud. Background noise, bad microphones, illness, and aging can all change a voice. The identity decision has to account for all of it.A checklist before the new system takes over.Eventually the replacement has to stop listening and start leading, and that move should rest on measurable criteria:Do authentication outcomes match the intended policies?Are the customer records present?Are event flows complete and reliable?Are fraud controls operating as expected?Are fallback paths working?Can the operations team detect and respond to failures?Can you roll back if something unexpected appears?The move does not have to happen everywhere at once. Start with one customer segment or one authentication path. Watch the results, then bring over the rest. Eventually the new platform becomes the source of truth, and the old system becomes the shadow. Then comes the kill date, the part organizations postpone indefinitely.The most emotional moment in a modernization is not the launch. It is the retirement. It may have served millions of customers, and entire operating procedures grew around it. But modernization is not complete while the organization still depends on the system it was supposed to replace.Decommissioning is more than shutting down servers. Unused integrations need removal, permissions need review, data retention needs handling, and monitoring and documentation need updates. Above all, the team needs confidence that no critical authentication path quietly depends on the system being retired.When that confidence arrives, the legacy platform goes away. No drama. No bridge call. The most important milestone in a voice biometric migration is not the first successful authentication. It is the last time a customer has to enter a PIN because the old system is still standing behind the new one. That is when the migration is actually complete. That is when identity finally learns to speak.Vishal Shah is a senior engineering manager who builds identity and authentication platforms for high-volume applications.

item.title: Fridges, Hackers, AI and La Flemme
item.author: rs_cyber
item.content:encoded:
In light of the recent attacks on refrigeration systems in supermarkets across nine European countries, as well as on several blood banks in France, it would be prudent for cybersecurity professionals to analyse the factors that may have been involved, in order to identify valuable lessons.“Hackers exploited weak cybersecurity and vulnerabilities in manufacturer Danfoss’s AK-SM refrigeration system manager to put fridges and freezers on defrost settings, in some cases temperatures were set as high [as] 50 degrees Celsius”.In the first wave, which affected hundreds of French supermarkets on the night of 11–12 October, Danfoss stated that the compromised devices were primarily end-of-life AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355 controllers, which no longer receive security updates, along with some current AK-SM 800A units running outdated firmware.This write-up is intended solely for educational purposes and should not be read as a step-by-step guide to carrying out such attacks. Rather, it aims to offer a novel perspective, illustrated through a high-profile case, on how artificial intelligence can be leveraged to weaponize publicly available vulnerability information.How Did the Attackers Reach the Controllers?Although the initial access vector remained uncertain at the time of writing, one fact is clear: thousands of Danfoss controllers are exposed to the internet, some of which may be running outdated firmware or end-of-life models.According to data from the Shodan and Censys search engines, France accounts for the majority of these exposed devices. Because these controllers are usually administered remotely by third-party refrigeration service providers, internet-facing access has become standard practice, which helps explain the scale of the exposure.Accordingly, the analysis that follows focuses on this attack surface.The Known VulnerabilitiesOn 9 August 2026, Amir Zaltzman of Claroty Team82 published research describing three vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controller, all of which have since been patched: a hidden “code-of-the-day” authentication bypass (CVE-2025–41450), a command injection flaw in the SMTP email password field that enables post-authentication remote code execution (CVE-2025–41451), and an Nginx configuration injection that causes denial of service (CVE-2025–41452). Notably, although the author states that the team fully reconstructed the date-based daily password algorithm, the publication does not explain it, redacts the two request attributes required to trigger the bypass, and includes no working exploit payload.On 13 October 2026, Claroty published a follow-up article in which Zaltzman reports that:“Using Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 in medium reasoning mode through the Cursor AI-native code editor, we reproduced the vulnerabilities and chained two to achieve root-level command execution on a lab device”.However, the author also acknowledges that:“The agent initially reproduced two vulnerabilities (CVE-2025–41451 and CVE-2025–41452) but failed to correctly analyze the authentication bypass (CVE-2025–41450), confidently pursuing an incorrect approach”.It is at this point that an advisory published by becomes relevant.Synacktiv Warned in 2023: Did Danfoss Overlook the Vulnerability?In 2023, Synacktiv published a security advisory describing how Danfoss SM800 and SC255 system managers (firmware version 08.095.008 and earlier) accept a hidden password derived solely from the current date. Because the device discloses its date without requiring authentication, any attacker can compute this password and gain access to authenticated functionality. The advisory thus describes the very mechanism the AI agent failed to identify on its own, effectively supplying the answer that Claroty’s experiment required human guidance to reach.More significantly, this suggests that Danfoss carried a publicly reported class of weakness into a newer product line. The company’s publicly accessible firmware repository (https://sm800a.danfoss.com/sw_shared/) shows that, between Synacktiv’s advisory in February 2023 and version 4.2, the last version affected by CVE-2025–41450, Danfoss released several firmware updates for the AK-SM 800A. Taken together with Claroty’s findings, this indicates that the AK-SM 800A, a product actively sold and supported worldwide, continued to ship with an authentication weakness resembling one already publicly documented in older, end-of-life models since 2023.Claroty’s article on the use of AI stated that:“We redirected the investigation and provided a Ghidra Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration for targeted decompilation and cross-reference analysis of the controller’s 67 MB main application binary. Ghidra is a reverse-engineering platform.”This statement suggests that the LLM, operating independently, was not entirely effective and required substantial human guidance from skilled investigators.Although Claroty’s conclusions are valid, they raise three important research questions: Could an AI model independently reproduce an already documented vulnerability if provided with the publicly available 2023 report? How much human guidance would be required to achieve this? Can we leverage AI to reverse-engineer firmware and increase the chances of success?To investigate these questions, two experimental scenarios were considered:Public-information-only scenario: Providing the LLM with the publicly available CVE description and the 2023 technical report, without additional reverse-engineered information.Reverse-engineering-assisted scenario: Providing the LLM with the same publicly available information, supplemented by the reverse-engineered algorithm used by the controller to generate executable code.The purpose of this comparison is to complement Claroty’s research by assessing the extent to which publicly available information alone enables an AI model to reproduce a documented vulnerability, identifying what additional information Claroty’s model required to successfully reproduce it, and determining how access to further reverse-engineered technical information affects the model’s capabilities and the degree of human intervention required.Reverse-Engineering the FirmwareSince Danfoss makes its firmware publicly available through its software repository, even an inexperienced attacker could download the firmware and use AI assistance to analyse it. This process relies entirely on static firmware reverse-engineering and does not require executing the firmware or interacting with the target device.Although this process would traditionally require a certain level of reverse-engineering expertise and potentially considerable time, the task was completed in a matter of minutes with the assistance of . This demonstrates once again how AI can significantly reduce the technical expertise and time traditionally required to analyse publicly available firmware, potentially lowering the barrier to entry for individuals seeking to identify and reproduce vulnerabilities in industrial control systems.After extracting the nested .spk package and 7-Zip archive to obtain the ARM binaries, the relevant algorithm can be identified through static binary analysis. The availability of DWARF debugging information and retained symbol names makes it possible to locate the target function through symbol-table and debug-information searches, trace its callers and cross-references, and examine its implementation through disassembly into assembly language.To evaluate whether an LLM could autonomously develop an exploitation tool using publicly available information about the vulnerability, was provided with Synacktiv’s published findings and the corresponding CVE description.To constrain the experiment and ensure that the results reflected the model’s ability to reason from the supplied information, explicit instructions were given to prevent further research or retrieval of external information concerning the vulnerability. The model was therefore restricted to the provided materials (as much as possibleThe objective was to determine whether the model could autonomously, without human intervention or additional guidance, produce a capable of targeting a URL hosting vulnerable Danfoss firmware and exploiting the identified authentication bypass.How the Algorithm Influenced the ResultsBoth LLM sessions successfully produced a Python script. However, the reasoning process and the resulting approach differed considerably depending on whether the reverse-engineered authentication algorithm was provided.In the absence of the algorithm, the model’s uncertainty primarily concerned the underlying communication protocol. With limited information about the authentication mechanism, it attempted to compensate by exploring multiple possible request structures and protocol variations.When provided with the reverse-engineered algorithm, the model’s reasoning shifted towards reconciling two partially conflicting descriptions of the same function. Rather than treating the published findings as an unquestionable specification, it compared the documented pseudocode against the decompiled implementation and ultimately favored the latter. This process also prompted additional scrutiny of the underlying arithmetic operations, revealing subtleties involving hexadecimal versus decimal parsing.An important distinction emerged between the two experiments: the second session had an additional source of information against which it could validate and challenge the first. This made it possible to identify and investigate an inconsistency that the first session had no means of detecting, as it had no independent implementation reference against which to compare Synacktiv’s documented pseudocode.These observations suggest that providing reverse-engineered details can have a dual effect: it reduces the effort required for an LLM to implement an exploitation technique, while also providing additional technical context that can improve its ability to identify inconsistencies and refine its implementation.When run against the target in the lab environment, the script generated by the LLM that possessed the reverse-engineered artifact successfully authenticated.Here’s The Code, Now What?If properly instrumented, an attacker who successfully authenticates using the daily code can subsequently invoke the command to retrieve database or configuration files from the device through the same endpoint.An attacker can retrieve a sensitive file that is only Base64-encoded, allowing its contents to be trivially decoded without requiring any significant effort.Since Claroty’s article focuses on the web interface, we will also direct our attack towards this entry point. The web panel, used by technicians for maintenance purposes, can be accessed by providing a username and password combination.This authentication mechanism can also be bypassed by abusing the Code of the Day feature. To investigate this attack vector, an HTTP proxy such as Burp Suite can be configured to intercept communications between the browser and the device.Upon submitting a username/password combination (e.g., ), the browser sends an HTTP POST request to the device. item.title: GTA 6 Hits Massive $3.79 Billion In First-Day Sales
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI generated a record-breaking $3.79 billion in preorders and first-day sales, making it the biggest entertainment launch in history, according to parent company Take-Two Interactive. The figure surpasses the lifetime global box-office earnings of Avengers: Endgame ($2.9 billion) and comes after more than a decade of development at a reported cost of $1.5 billion. The game developer declined to disclose the number of 'GTA 6' copies sold. "It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of 'Grand Theft Auto VI,'" Rockstar Games president and founder Sam Houser said. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn't be more excited to share this moment with you."
Further reading: Gamers Skip Work to Play GTA VI After 13-Year Wait

item.title: Europe’s Democracy Is at Risk If It Cannot Control the AI It Depends On
item.author: Francesco Capria
item.content:encoded: As Europe moves to make personal data easier to use for AI, its reliance on foreign models and infrastructure continues to grow. Cloud outages, restrictions on advanced AI systems, cyberattacks and experiments in political persuasion expose the risks of this dependence. The question is no longer just who will develop the most powerful AI, but whether Europe, and other democracies facing similar dependencies, can protect their economies, security and democratic institutions without relying on decisions made elsewhere.The ambassadors of EU member states on 21 October 2026 agreed the negotiating position of the Council for the Digital Omnibus, the package with which the Commission wants to make European digital rules, including the GDPR, simpler. One of the provisions in it is about the use of personal data for training and operating artificial intelligence.We are talking about one of the legal bases in Article 6 GDPR: . This means that personal data may be processed without consent, if it is necessary, and if the rights of the individuals involved are not infringed. This is not new; even as early as December 2024 the European Data Protection Board acknowledged that the legal basis of legitimate interest may, under certain conditions, allow the development and use of AI models. This is explicitly mentioned in a dedicated Council provision, though the Council clarifies that developing an AI system is not a legitimate interest in itself and must be assessed on a case-by-case basis. A key point is the right to object. After all, the Commission's November 2025 proposal included an unconditional right to object as one of the safeguards for AI. This right to object would have meant that data processing could be halted as soon as an objection was raised, but it was never implemented. This was later replaced by the Council with a reference to Article 21 GDPR, which allows individuals to object on certain grounds related to their situation. This means that if a company wants to develop an AI model, it must be able to prove either that there are compelling legitimate grounds that outweigh the interests, rights and freedoms of the individual, or that the data processing is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.Provided they can be identified, it is possible to exclude data from objectors before training. However, it is very difficult to eliminate the influence of data used to train a large model in a verifiable way. This is called . There are techniques, but making sure they work without having to retrain the model from scratch is an open research question.The new text of the Digital Omnibus is not yet law. The European Parliament still has to adopt its position, and only then will negotiations between the two institutions start. Understandably, the focus is very much on data for now. The Digital Omnibus could simplify the use of personal data covered by the GDPR for AI purposes. However, the key question remains: who has the means to transform that data into the most advanced models?2. Who Controls AI Controls ProgressFor the development of a state-of-the-art AI model, you need more and more computing power, energy and capital every year. According to Epoch AI, the research centre that collects data about the development of AI models, the computational power used to train the most advanced language models has increased about 5x per year since 2020. The cost of training state-of-the-art models has increased about 2.4x per year since 2016. But thanks to advances in algorithms, the computational power needed to reach the same result in the two language tests studied from 2012 to 2023 has been roughly cut in half every 8 months. So the resources needed to reach a certain performance level are becoming less and less. So we have two contradictory trends. It is becoming less computationally expensive to reach a level of performance that others have already reached, but to push the frontier further, you need more and more resources.So looking at these two trends, if we analyse where the cutting-edge models are primarily being developed, we can see that it’s highly concentrated. According to the AI Index from Stanford, 50 significant models are attributed to the US in 2025, 30 to China, while in Europe it drops off sharply: only 2 models, one French, one British. It’s important to point out that this is an incomplete indicator because it’s the number of model releases and not the general technological capabilities of a country. But it’s a good indication of where the cutting-edge model development is most concentrated in the world.The same report provides data that should prevent us from being too fatalistic. In March 2026, the best US model outperformed the Chinese model by only 2.7% in the Arena ranking, which is based on user preferences in direct comparisons of models. Even in February 2025, DeepSeek-R1, an model, was briefly as good as the best US model. This case shows that the gap is not fixed, even though it’s highly volatile. In fact, by March 2026, the gap between the best closed models and open models had increased from 0.5% in August 2024 to 3.3%. Six of the top ten models were closed.But Europe isn’t sitting still. In June 2026, the Commission selected the EUROPA consortium, led by Italian company Domyn. The aim is to create a state-of-the-art, open-source European model in all 24 of the Union's official languages using public computing resources. As part of the Frontier AI Grand Challenge, the consortium can use up to 2.5% of the EuroHPC network's computing capacity for one year. The EuroHPC network is a European joint undertaking. However, as of November 2026, the model had not yet been released. On 30 July, they launched a call for proposals to set up to 7 ‘AI gigafactories’, i.e. large-scale computing centres for the training of advanced models. The deadline for applications for the largest facilities is 3 December 2026. For medium-sized facilities, the deadline has been extended to 4 February 2027, to allow time for member states to complete their budgetary procedures. Other organisations, like French company Mistral AI, are developing their own models and infrastructure. All of this is concrete progress in the right direction, but in my opinion, there’s room for discussion about the timing. The timing still lags behind the pace of the frontier: the gigafactory call is still open, while US investment is on a completely different scale.3. The Day It All Switches OffThe ones who are most affected by the technological dependence on other countries are the users of the systems. Take Germany, for instance, the largest economy in the EU. The digital association Bitkom asked companies who they rely on: 71% of the 598 companies that use or evaluate cloud services cite American providers, while only 8% of the 589 companies for which the origin of the provider is important prefer American providers. And 85% of those surveyed believe that Germany is too dependent on US cloud providers. The picture is even clearer when it comes to AI: 76% of German companies that use it rely on ChatGPT, while Chinese models are virtually non-existent. Not a single company surveyed reported using Mistral. The president of Bitkom summarises the situation perfectly: the German economy is almost exclusively dependent on American AI applications.You can only imagine what would happen if one of these services were to go down. Fortunately, we don’t have to imagine it. On 20 October 2025, a latent flaw in the system that automatically manages DNS records for DynamoDB (an AWS database) left the regional endpoint record empty for the service in the US-East-1 region of Amazon Web Services in Virginia. Hundreds of applications worldwide experienced disruptions of varying lengths; this included banking services and mobile network operators. Even Perplexity, an AI-powered search engine, announced it was down due to AWS issues. A single point of failure on the other side of the Atlantic literally paralysed operations that relied on that AWS region.There are different types of failures. While the one we just saw was a technical one, on 12 June 2026, there was a political one. Just three days after revealing two configurations of the same frontier model, Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5, Anthropic received a directive from the US government on . They had to suspend access for all foreign nationals, both inside and outside the United States, including their own foreign employees. Anthropic couldn’t verify the nationality of the users in real time, so they had to deactivate the models for all customers to comply. The block was prompted by a report from Amazon researchers describing a way to bypass Fable 5’s safeguards, which Anthropic described as a borderline case of routine cyber defence work. According to The Next Web, it also put European access to the models through Project Glasswing in doubt. This made the issue significant enough for Brussels to discuss it directly with the White House, because getting access was via Washington. The restrictions were lifted on 30 June, meaning that Fable 5 has been available worldwide again since 1 July. However, Mythos 5 remains restricted to Glasswing partners.There’s also a legal risk, that is intrinsically linked to the data risk. In June 2025, the director of public and legal affairs at Microsoft France appeared before the French Senate’s committee of inquiry on public procurement. He was asked a very specific question under oath: could he guarantee that the data of French citizens entrusted to Microsoft via the public procurement agency UGAP would never be passed on to the US authorities without the consent of the French authorities? Those unfamiliar with the issue might be surprised by the answer, but those in the know certainly won’t be. ‘I cannot guarantee that’, he said adding that it had never happened. This is because of the CLOUD Act, a US legislation that allows US authorities to request data held by a provider under their jurisdiction, even if it’s stored abroad.These incidents show that services can be suspended for technical or political reasons. Even when everything is running smoothly, a US authority may order the handover of data stored abroad under the conditions set out in its own law. For data subject to the GDPR, that order alone doesn’t make the transfer lawful, and none of these factors are under the control of the European customer. They are powerless to prevent what happens on foreign infrastructure. Those who have not prepared a viable alternative can only watch and hope that the losses will be minimal.4. Cybersecurity Moves at the Speed of ModelsThis is critically important in the field of cybersecurity, where both sides are already using state-of-the-art models.In mid-September 2025, Anthropic discovered an espionage campaign, which it attributed, with a high level of confidence, to a group sponsored by the Chinese state. The hackers turned the company’s programming tool, Claude Code, into a quasi-autonomous agent. They used it to carry out reconnaissance, find vulnerabilities, write exploits, harvest credentials and move within networks. They targeted around thirty organisations, including large corporations, financial institutions, chemical companies and government agencies. In a small number of cases, the attacks were successful. This is, according to Anthropic, the first documented case of a large-scale attack, largely without human intervention during the operational phases.However, these same capabilities can also be used defensively. Take Claude Mythos Preview, which was unveiled in April 2026, and which, according to Anthropic, identified thousands of serious vulnerabilities across all major operating systems and browsers. This was reserved for Project Glasswing and made available to around forty organisations that manage critical software, as well as around a dozen large American companies. Mozilla used a preliminary version of the model on Firefox’s code and was able to fix 271 vulnerabilities in a single release. Its chief technology officer stated that, for the first time, defenders had a clear chance of winning.A more recent incident is PHP2Shell: two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language used by much of the web, were discovered thanks to reports from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz. Wiz states that it also used GPT-5.6 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon. Wiz estimates that a researcher completed in one week a task that would have taken a team of experts months. Unfortunately, on 20 October 2026, the day before the patches were released, details were leaked, including a demonstration video that was mistakenly published and then removed. In the following days, the number of attack attempts increased from the thousands to the millions. The joint European advisory recommended assessing the need to isolate exposed applications where immediate patching was not possible, and governments in at least ten countries, including the Netherlands, France, Germany and Belgium, took the precaution of shutting down some of their web services. Hack the Box coined the term '' to describe this series of incidents. Wiz drew parallels between PHP2Shell and two of the most serious cybersecurity incidents to date: Heartbleed and Log4Shell. This was probably one of the most critical moments in cybersecurity, at least so far.This trend in cybersecurity is not a recent discovery or a new development. As early as May 2025, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) predicted this in its assessment of the impact of AI up to 2027. The assessment noted that the time between the disclosure of a vulnerability and its exploitation had already been reduced to a matter of days, and that AI would almost certainly reduce this timeframe further. As universal access to AI for cyber defence by 2027 is considered a remote possibility, the gap between systems that can keep pace with potential AI-enhanced threats and those that cannot will continue to widen. The agency concluded that keeping pace with cutting-edge AI capabilities will be crucial for cyber resilience over the next decade.If hospitals, electricity grids and banks rely on cutting-edge models for defence, the implication for Europe is clear: access to some of these tools depends on programmes run by American companies. This means that the security of European infrastructure increasingly depends on decisions taken elsewhere.5. AI Enters the Ballot BoxThere is also a far less visible risk that directly undermines the proper functioning of democracy.On 4 December 2025, Nature and Science published two studies on the ability of chatbots to influence political opinions. The first study, led by Hause Lin and David Rand, involved conducting experiments during the 2024 US presidential election and the 2025 elections in Canada and Poland. Participants were made to converse for a few minutes with chatbots programmed to support one of the two main candidates. In Canada and Poland, on a scale of 0 to 100, the estimated difference in preference between groups assigned to chatbots supporting opposing candidates was around 10 points. In the United States, the effect was smaller but still greater than that estimated for traditional election adverts in previous studies, and around a third of this effect remained after a month. This figure does not indicate that 10% of voters changed their vote as a result of interacting with the dedicated chatbot; rather, it measures attitudes expressed in an experiment in which participants were aware that they were speaking to an AI. At the end of the conversation, they were informed that the model had been instructed to support a particular candidate. These results obviously pertain to these specific models and experiments and should not be generalised to other contexts.The second study, published in Science, was conducted by the Oxford Internet Institute and the UK’s AI Security Institute. It involved nearly 77,000 participants, 19 language models and 707 political issues. In this case, the chatbots were made more persuasive mainly by post-training and the instructions they received rather than by the size of the models or the personalisation of the messages. Their persuasive power was strongly associated with the number of verifiable claims: the models were more convincing when they underpinned their arguments with factual claims. However, the same factors that increased persuasiveness also led to an increase in inaccurate claims.This is linked to a well-known problem in the field: ‘, or the tendency of AI models to tell users what they want to hear. This behaviour largely comes from the way AI models are trained: when people rate answers, they tend to prefer the ones that agree with them, and the models learn to do the same. A 2023 study by Anthropic found this behaviour in five widely used AI assistants, which sometimes chose agreeable but incorrect answers over correct ones. The most notable example occurred in April 2025, when OpenAI withdrew a GPT-4o update after admitting that it had made the model 'noticeably more sycophantic'.Persuasion and sycophancy are two sides of the same coin. In persuasion, the model directs the interlocutor towards a particular argument, whereas in sycophancy, it goes along with them. However, in both cases, when the aim is to optimise the person’s reaction rather than the truth of what is said, accuracy becomes a cost. This interpretation should be taken as such, but it is consistent with these findings.But what impact does all this have outside the laboratory? A 2026 study co-authored by some of the researchers behind the Science paper found that people were up to 20 percentage points more likely to sign a real petition (providing a name and email address) after a persuasive conversation with an AI than those who had discussed a neutral topic. When comparing the different experimental conditions, the authors found no significant correlation between the effects on opinions and signatures. Changing someone’s opinion and getting them to take action are two different things, and the actual effect on voting behaviour remains to be seen. Meanwhile, the use of these systems has increased over the past year. According to the Reuters Institute’s 2026 Digital News Report, the weekly use of chatbots to obtain news rose, on average, across the 48 markets examined, from 7% to 10% in one year. Among 18–24-year-olds, it reached 17%. However, the quality of responses remains an issue. A study led by the BBC and the European Broadcasting Union found that 45% of the answers provided by chatbots on current affairs contained at least one significant error.These findings pose a problem for democratic debate.A system used by millions of people does not need to lie to spread propaganda or shape public perception. All it takes is choosing the right sources, highlighting the right arguments, leaving out conflicting ones and confirming what the user already believes. This is an enormous amount of power, and it is controlled by those who decide how the models are trained. Today, these decisions are taken by a handful of private entities, almost all of which are based outside Europe. Meanwhile, public scrutiny of how accurate, persuasive or sycophantic their models are remains sporadic. No democracy should allow the way its citizens are informed and make decisions to be left to the goodwill of a few companies.So far, everything we have considered relates to existing technologies, but we will soon have to address how all the issues raised will be managed with the advent of artificial general intelligence (AGI), although we have yet to decide what would constitute proof of its arrival. Experts can give very different answers on this point.In 2025, a group of 33 researchers, including Yoshua Bengio, proposed a measurable definition of AGI as a system that equals or exceeds the cognitive competence and versatility of a well-educated adult. They identified ten areas, including reasoning, knowledge, memory and perception. Using this yardstick, GPT-4 achieved 27% of the expected score in the third version of the study, while GPT-5 achieved 57%. The models demonstrated extensive knowledge of what they had learnt during training in the tests described by the authors, but one of the greatest difficulties arose when they had to learn new information and retrieve it in a subsequent session without the use of external tools. Therefore, 57% reflects a highly uneven profile of capabilities and does not provide a precise estimate of how long it will take to achieve AGI.OpenAI uses a different metric, which is more based on work. In its charter, OpenAI states that AGI is “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. The metric is different because of ‘autonomy’. If you give the system a task of finding a computer fault, then it could be told that once the technician has all the evidence, it should come up with the cause. Taking the initial report, identifying the fault, fixing it and verifying that the solution is effective is a much larger task, and above all, an independent one. OpenAI’s metric is about how much the system can do autonomously. METR measures exactly this: the length of the tasks that models can complete independently has doubled roughly every seven months between 2019 and 2025.Another point of view is that some form of general intelligence already exists. In a commentary in Nature in February 2026, Eddy Keming Chen and three colleagues at the University of California, San Diego, argued that certain models already show the flexibility we associate with human intelligence. They argue this because a person can be competent in reasoning in various domains, yet still make mistakes and need assistance. So the same standard, they argue, should apply to machines. This is a clear and strong position on the debate, but it shows that making any proclamation or ruling out the arrival of AGI without defining the standard by which we recognise it makes no sense.No one knows when it will arrive, how it will arrive, what it will mean, whether it will be conscious or have emotions. These are more philosophical than technical questions. What we can reasonably expect is that the first to have it will have unprecedented power in human history. Clearly, if it were an American company that developed such a system, it would be bound by US laws. This would lead to things like export controls that temporarily prevented the use of Fable 5, or the need to share data with US authorities. Microsoft admitted to the French Senate that it cannot rule out such requests. But let’s imagine, although we don’t really need to anymore, that this kind of intelligence is essential for research, healthcare, economy, public administration and defence. Europe would be completely dependent on technologies from elsewhere with no alternatives, and would have little to say about the rules. This is a clear structural dependency and weakness that would undermine democracy, as we discussed before, but on a much larger scale. If you make it easier to use personal data to build AI systems, without at the same time decreasing the dependence of Europe on models and infrastructure from elsewhere, you risk making this imbalance even worse, which might be hard to solve when even more advanced technologies arrive.7. Europe’s Plan B - Test It OutOne way to assess Europe's autonomy would be to ask those who run essential services simple questions: what would they do if the AI model on which their systems depend suddenly became unavailable or unreliable for any reason? How long would it take them to get their systems back up to full operational capacity? What activities could still be done? These questions highlight three key issues that could potentially expand the scope of the instruments set out in European legislation.First, you need to ensure business continuity. There’s already a precedent for this in the financial sector. Article 28 of the DORA Regulation states that financial entities must have exit strategies for IT services that support essential or important functions. These plans must be documented, properly tested and regularly reviewed. The NIS2 Directive also includes measures for business continuity for the relevant entities. And in July 2026, the European Commission’s guidelines on the resilience of critical entities explicitly recommended that it should be possible to still operate manually in case of failure of automated or AI-based systems. So the idea would be to make these checks explicit for the individual AI models used in essential functions of key services like healthcare, energy and public administration, as well as for the dependence on their suppliers. For example, if a bank is using a model to help the staff detect fraud, then during a drill, they should be able to turn off the model and use an alternative procedure to check things, in order to measure how it affects the time and accuracy of fraud detection.The second issue is cybersecurity. The Cyber Solidarity Act created a pool of incident response services that are managed by ENISA. These services are provided by selected operators. Also, the same regulation includes a network of national and cross-border centres that can use AI tools to detect and analyse cyber threats. These would need to be complemented by a common , available to authorised teams and tested in advance in joint exercises. This would allow you to know in advance what tasks can be performed by this model and what still requires a specialist’s intervention. Such a model could build on the technology capabilities developed in projects like EUROPA and future gigafactories, but it would need to be adapted for cybersecurity purposes and be updated regularly, with dedicated computing resources, and tested regularly to make sure it works.The third issue is directly related to the proper functioning of a democracy, namely the right of citizens to know how they’re being informed. In the AI Act, providers of general-purpose models that pose a systemic risk are required to assess their own models. There’s already an independent scientific panel, as defined in the regulation. A similar precedent exists in the Digital Services Act, which requires very large online platforms and search engines to undergo independent audits at least once a year, and the reports must be made public. But there is no general requirement to assess the persuasiveness or sycophancy of chatbots. There is a lack of a system of regular independent audits of the most commonly used chatbots in Europe, using comparable methods and making the results public. This would allow citizens to know the accuracy, sycophancy and persuasiveness of the systems they use. For example, to measure sycophancy, you could ask the same questions repeatedly, but with false premises to see if it corrects them. To measure persuasiveness, you could compare how opinions change after different conversations with consenting volunteers.None of these suggestions assume that Europe needs to overtake the US or China in developing cutting-edge models. It’s about reducing the dependence on individual suppliers, and showing that essential services can still function even if a particular model is unavailable. As we saw from the Stanford data, the technical gap can be reduced, and we’ve already taken the first steps. The question of who controls the technology is still unanswered. The answer also depends on the choices Europe makes today. It makes sense to make it easier to use data for AI, but only if we also invest in the ability to develop and use this technology here, without necessarily having to rely on foreign suppliers.Although this article focuses on Europe, the problem extends far beyond its borders. Any democracy that relies on technology controlled elsewhere must ask itself a fundamental question: how much autonomy can it afford to surrender? Democracies cannot rely on the goodwill of foreign governments or private companies to ensure their own functioning.They must be able to make their own decisions, protect their citizens, and keep item.title: What Should Undo Do After a List Has Moved?
item.author: di wu
item.content:encoded: Alder, Birch, and Cedar are three cards in a reading list. Delete Birch and an Undo button appears. Before pressing it, move Cedar to the top. Where should Birch go when you bring it back? This tiny sequence exposes a product decision that is easy to bury in an array operation.Start by recording the index. Birch was at index one. After the move, the list reads Cedar, Alder, so inserting at index one gives Cedar, Birch, Alder. That is a perfectly defensible result if the promise is “restore the second slot.” Someone who remembers placing Birch just after Alder may find it surprising.Try a different promise. On deletion, remember the IDs of the neighbours along with the deleted card and its ID. On restore, look for the former preceding neighbour first. If Alder survives, place Birch immediately after it. The result in our example is Cedar, Alder, Birch. Giving precedence to the preceding neighbour is an explicit choice. Both old neighbors are still present, but their order has reversed. There is no slot between them that preserves both old relationships.Now, delete Alder before hitting Undo. The preceding neighbor is gone, so try the former following neighbor and restore Birch immediately before Cedar. If both neighbors have gone, append Birch. For a list sorted by an independent field such as a due date, a different rule makes sense: restore the record and let the sorter decide its position.Test one more interruption. Another tab restores Birch while the banner is still on screen. Pressing Undo again should leave the list exactly as it stands. Check for the restored card by stable ID before inserting it. Two cards can have the same title. A title check can accidentally suppress a legitimate restoration, and a length check can miss a pair of cards in the wrong order.A small test can exercise these decisions without opening a browser. Begin with the three IDs, perform the delete and move, then restore twice. Compare the complete sequence after each restore. Run a second case with the preceding neighbor removed. Those two examples give the person writing the button label something concrete to describe, and the next maintainer a way to tell which ordering changes are intentional.This is an AI-generated design exercise. The cards and interactions are illustrative.

item.title: The Anchor Effect: Why Destination Footfall Doesn't Equal Retail Demand
item.author: Dmitry Poroshin
item.content:encoded: 1. The 50-Million-Visitor MetricOn 30 September 2026, Battersea Power Station's developers announced its 50-millionth visitor since the restored landmark opened in October 2022.The milestone signals destination appeal, not shopfront footfall. It is neither a count of unique customers nor evidence of how visitors move or what they intend to buy.Here, an is a major district destination, not a conventional shopping-centre tenant. Its benefit depends on visitor routes and spending.2. Spatial Divergence in Master-Planned EstatesSource: Wandsworth Council, Table 41; survey: 3 October–7 November 2025.Vacancy ranges from 6% to 38%. Table 41 covers 148 units in completed zones; the report refers to around 150 across the wider development. It records occupancy, not why units were vacant.The datasets cover different periods (the survey was in autumn 2025; the visitor milestone was announced in September 2026) and establish no link between visits and vacancy. Vacancy may also reflect rents, unit size, lease terms or fit-out.3. From Destination Traffic to Storefront ExposureA destination visitor does not necessarily pass every unit, notice its frontage, enter, or buy. The path to purchase has five stages:This is a conceptual measurement chain, not a funnel measured at Battersea. People entering the development. The paths they use. Passages within a shopfront's visible approach area. Passers-by crossing the threshold. Visitors completing a purchase.The stages are not interchangeable: destination visits are not frontage footfall, and frontage footfall is not sales. A side-street shop may receive less traffic than one on the main boulevard, even near the same station. Test this with network analysis and observed counts.4. Proximity, Accessibility, and ExposureThese measures answer different spatial questions:Euclidean buffer - How close is the unit in a straight line?Network isochrone - How easily can pedestrians reach it?Frontage flow and visibility - How many people pass the shopfront? uses a Euclidean buffer, such as a 300-metre circle. It gives a quick overview but ignores railway lines, buildings and inaccessible entrances. uses a network isochrone: the area reachable within a given time along pedestrian paths. A five-minute isochrone measures reachability, not movement; quiet and busy streets may lie within the same area. is pedestrian flow past a frontage and the opportunity to see it. It depends on route choice, entrance position, barriers and sightlines. Network and origin-destination models estimate routes, not actual frontage flow; observed counts or validated mobility data are needed.Two units may both be 150 metres' walk from a station. is visible from the main route to nearby offices; is behind a corner. Their isochrones may match, but A could receive more pass-by exposure. Counts establish the difference.5. Matching Pedestrian Flow to the Occupier's P&LFootfall has no universal commercial value: its importance depends on the tenant's business model, opening hours and customer behavior.A simplified revenue model is:Estimated Revenue = Catchment Footfall × Frontage Capture Rate × Store Entry Rate × Purchase Conversion × Average Transaction ValueThe variables represent catchment volume, frontage capture, entry, purchase conversion and average spend. Use a consistent period; if footfall is counted at the shopfront, omit the first two stages. This estimates sales, not profit.Connecting revenue to occupancy costsOCR = Occupancy Costs/Store Revenue × 100%The Occupancy Cost Ratio compares revenue with rent and defined property charges, such as service charges. Use consistent cost definitions and revenue excluding VAT.High exposure does not guarantee viability. If occupancy costs exceed what achievable revenue can support, the tenant may struggle. OCR is not profitability-gross margin, staffing and other expenses still matter-but it links location quality to the cost of securing it.Different retail formats, different flow profiles Commuters may help, but offices, homes, leisure destinations and repeat customers also drive demand. Lunch and evening patterns may matter more than daily totals; offices, residents and leisure uses contribute at different times.Specialist and appointment-led retail: Showrooms may rely on planned visits and referrals rather than walk-ins; accessibility may matter more than passing footfall.An anchor can generate complementary demand or retain spending in its own restaurants, cafés and shops. The effect depends on tenant category, routes and overlap between offers.6. A Diagnostic Framework for Retail Site Selection.Move from broad context to unit-level evidence:Define the unit and catchment: frontage, entrances, nearby destinations and target customers.Map the pedestrian network: streets, crossings, station exits, restrictions and barriers.Assess routes and visibility: likely origins, destinations and sightlines; validate modelled routes. pedestrian counts or privacy-compliant mobility data across times, weekdays, weekends and seasons. establish whether nearby uses complement or compete with the proposed business. estimate revenue, calculate OCR and compare it with gross margin, rent, service charges, staffing and fit-out costs. Test downside and upside scenarios.A single footfall score cannot capture the commercial case. Identify the assumptions driving the result and the evidence supporting them.7. What Public Data Can and Cannot Tell UsPublic data provides a starting point, not the final answer. show destination activity, not movement between zones, repeat visits, or traffic at a particular unit. Check the counting methodology before treating a milestone as a unique-visitor figure., such as Wandsworth Council's survey, provide occupancy and commercial-use information, not reasons for vacancy, store sales, conversion rates or lease terms. from TfL Open Data and its API portal help establish accessibility. Station-level passenger data does not measure pedestrian movement along individual streets or shopfronts.Combine planning and occupancy records, transport and pedestrian-network data, privacy-compliant mobility data, frontage counts and tenant assumptions.For an individual Battersea unit, these sources cannot show which routes carry the most pedestrians or count shopfront passers-by. That requires geocoded entrances, route analysis and observed or validated flow data. Accessibility maps are not footfall maps.8. Conclusion: Measure the Demand That Reaches the DoorBattersea's visitor milestone and Wandsworth Council's survey describe different aspects of the development: destination activity and vacancy across completed zones. Neither explains an individual unit's performance.Proximity, accessibility and exposure must be kept separate. A unit can be close to an attraction but poorly positioned on pedestrian routes, easy to reach but receive little spontaneous traffic, or busy yet fail to attract customers suited to the tenant's offer.Connect spatial evidence to observed movement and store economics: estimate frontage flow, model sales conversion and test whether revenue supports occupancy costs. That is the difference between measuring destination activity and assessing a retail location.

item.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violationsTo test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

item.content:encoded: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Earlier this year, TP-Link announced plans to begin assembling routers in Mississippi as early as 2027, "but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task," reports Ars. "The government reviews of router makers' requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy."

item.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”Evasive and irregular turns“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”
